Give every tree Entire writes to a single os.Root anchor
Entire does filesystem I/O in six trees, and until now each read and write
assembled its own absolute path and handed it to os.ReadFile/os.WriteFile.
Containment was therefore a property each call site had to keep honouring
by hand, and several of them carried comments saying so outright:
PluginDataDir "guarantees ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR always points inside the
managed data subtree", investigate.RunDir noted that "an unvalidated id
would be a path-traversal sink" feeding os.RemoveAll.

Each tree now has one package that owns a shared *os.Root over it, and the
names that reach those roots are relative to them:

  .entire                    entiredir
  git common dir             gitdir
  the working tree           worktreedir
  an agent's session store   agent.SessionStore
  per-user config / cache    userdirs.ConfigRoot / CacheRoot
  managed plugin tree        pluginRoot

The roots memoize through one registry, osroot.Shared, replacing three
separate copies of that map. Directory creation goes through
osroot.MkdirAllNoSymlink, which refuses a component that already exists as
a symlink -- os.Root blocks a symlink that escapes a root but follows one
pointing elsewhere inside it, and an escaping one otherwise surfaces as an
opaque errno far from the cause. entire doctor reports the symlinks that
are already there.

Two anchors are worth calling out because they close a real gap rather
than formalising an existing one. agent.SessionStore is where a hook
payload's session ID becomes a path via the agent's own
ResolveSessionFile; SessionFile converts the result back to a name inside
the store and rejects an ID that walked out of it, which a plain
filepath.Join produced silently. worktreedir covers the checkpoint tree
entries rewind restores, which may have been fetched from a remote --
rewind's restore half already opened a root for that reason; the reads
beside it did not.

paths.WorktreeRoot is now the single answer to "where is the repository",
and entiredir.anchor falls back to the current directory only on git's
positive ErrNotARepository verdict. The fallback it replaces fired on any
resolve failure, `git` off $PATH included, and then silently gave an agent
working in a subdirectory of a real repo its own .entire beside itself. A
root is only as trustworthy as the directory it is opened on, so a base
that cannot be resolved is not a base to guess at.

settings.readConfined keeps its symlink refusal on every branch, through
one readConfinedIn: the .entire branch briefly read straight through
osroot.ReadFile, which follows an in-root symlink silently -- precisely
the .entire/settings.local.json -> planted.json case the check exists for.

Rename the rewind-point identifiers to pending checkpoints
#2178 removed the rewind restore path, but the listing machinery that
survived it kept the name. What `checkpoint list --pending` returns is a
pending checkpoint: a shadow-branch checkpoint not yet condensed onto
entire/checkpoints/v1. Nothing about it rewinds anything.

Pure rename, 119 identifier uses across 20 files:

  RewindPoint             -> PendingCheckpoint          (63)
  ResolveAgentForRewind   -> ResolveAgentForResume      (19)
  GetRewindPoints         -> ListPendingCheckpoints     (15)
  pendingRewindPointJSON  -> pendingCheckpointJSON       (7)
  rewindPointLabel        -> pendingCheckpointLabel      (4)
  pendingRewindPointsLimit-> pendingCheckpointsLimit     (4)
  GetLogsOnlyRewindPoints -> ListLogsOnlyPendingCheckpoints (3)
  getImportedRewindPoints -> getImportedPendingCheckpoints  (3)
  RewindPoints            -> PendingCheckpoints          (1)

Get- became List- because these return a slice and take a limit;
ResolveAgentForRewind became ForResume because all three of its callers
are resume commands (newResumeCmd, newCheckpointResumeCmd,
newTrailResumeCmd).

No gopls on this machine, so the renames went through word-boundary
regex, longest name first so that GetRewindPoints and
GetLogsOnlyRewindPoints could not be shredded by the RewindPoint pass,
with `go build ./...` gating each step. Word boundaries also mean test
function names were skipped (TestResolveAgentForRewind has no boundary
before Resolve), so those were renamed separately:
TestShadowStrategy_GetRewindPoints_* and TestResolveAgentForRewind, plus
the file-local writeCommittedRewindCheckpoint helper (now
writeCommittedCheckpoint -- it writes a committed checkpoint, not a
pending one) and two test agent fixture strings.

File moves via git mv: manual_commit_rewind.go -> manual_commit_pending.go,
and rewind_test.go -> restore_logs_test.go. The second name is not
manual_commit_pending_test.go on purpose: every test left in that file
exercises the log-restore/resume half (RestoreLogsOnly, prompt preview,
FirstDisplayPrompt, ResolveAgentForResume), while the listing half is
tested in manual_commit_test.go.

The wire format is untouched, and could not have moved: every field in
pendingCheckpointJSON carries an explicit json tag, so renaming the Go
type leaves `checkpoint list --pending --json` byte-identical. No JSON
key ever contained "rewind" -- `grep 'json:"[^"]*rewind'` is empty across
the tree. Flag names, command paths and aliases are also unchanged;
TestPendingCheckpointJSON_MatchesRewindListContract keeps its historical
suffix because the contract it pins really is the one `rewind --list`
produced.

Comments and user-facing strings are deliberately left for the next
commit, so this one is reviewable as a mechanical diff.

content.text:
Yes. The original bug is an implicit assumption:

> “Text that looks like metadata was intentionally supplied as metadata.”

That assumption becomes dangerous only when the result controls a consequential action.

I did a targeted graph-backed audit of the Go code. Most remaining whole-message checkpoint parsing is used only for discovery, attribution, status, review context, and dispatch. Those uses appear consistent with the new contract. But I found several assumptions worth investigating.

| Assumption | Where | Assessment |
|---|---|---|
| Trailer writer and reader recognize the same grammar | [trailers.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:241) | Likely bug |
| Multiple final checkpoint trailers have one clear winner | [trailers.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:150), [attach.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/attach.go:651) | Inconsistent policy |
| An existing body-mentioned checkpoint is suitable for explicit resume | [checkpoint_resume.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint_resume.go:187) | Deliberate residual risk |
| Shadow-branch commit messages are inherently trustworthy | [trailers.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:75), [ephemeral.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/checkpoint/ephemeral.go:209) | Needs boundary review |
| “Latest checkpoint” means greatest stored `CreatedAt` | [manual_commit_pending.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/strategy/manual_commit_pending.go:290) | Explicit but important assumption |

The strongest new candidate is a writer–reader disagreement.

The writer trims leading whitespace when deciding whether a paragraph is already a trailer block:

```go
last := strings.TrimSpace(lines[i])
if IsTrailerLine(last) {
    // treat as a trailer block
}
```

But the strict reader correctly does not trim leading whitespace.

Given:

```text
Subject

  Entire-Checkpoint: A
```

the writer may append `B` without inserting a separating blank line:

```text
Subject

  Entire-Checkpoint: A
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

The strict reader then rejects the entire paragraph because its first line is indented. Entire appears to have added `B`, but later mutation paths cannot recognize it. That looks like a genuine correctness gap; it is inferred from current code and does not appear covered by the existing tests.

There is also a multiple-trailer disagreement:

```text
Entire-Checkpoint: A
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

- The singular strict parser returns the first: `A`.
- Attach deliberately selects the last: `B`.

Therefore PostCommit/explain generation and attach can interpret the same final block differently. Entire normally produces one checkpoint trailer, so this is an edge case, but ambiguity should probably be rejected or resolved centrally.

The replay’s recorded intent explicitly accepts another assumption for compatibility: body IDs may be resume candidates if corresponding checkpoint data exists. Existence does not authenticate the association—someone can name a real checkpoint—but `entire checkpoint resume <commit>` is an explicit user operation that reads that checkpoint and restores local state. That is a conscious trade-off, not an unnoticed parser mistake.

Finally, `ParseSession`, `ParseMetadata`, and `ParseTaskMetadata` still search anywhere and return the first occurrence. Their callers assume ephemeral shadow commits were generated by Entire. That assumption deserves examination because the leading commit text originates from a cleaned user prompt and could contain trailer-shaped text.

So yes: this PR fixes one instance of a broader recurring pattern:

```text
Recognizable syntax
        ↓
Assumed provenance or intent
        ↓
Consequential behavior
```

The next useful investigation would be the writer–reader mismatch first; it is the most concrete newly identified gap. No files were changed during this audit.

---

# Handoff

Write a clipboard-ready prompt for another agent to investigate, discuss, or work
on a specific task.

Use when the user asks for `handoff <task>`, "write a handoff", "delegate this",
or wants a prompt for another agent.

## Workflow

1. Identify the task from the user text. If the user gives only a short label,
   infer from the current repo, recent discussion, branch name, linked issue/PR,
   docs, and obvious nearby context.
2. Gather enough context to write a useful handoff: repo/product identity,
   relevant issue/PR/branch names, likely modules, constraints, and known
   symptoms. Do not perform the receiving agent's full independent review or
   decide the final technical direction for them.
3. Write a standalone prompt for a fresh agent.
4. Copy the full prompt to the clipboard.
5. Final reply: terse confirmation with the task title. Do not paste the full
   prompt unless the user asks.

## Handoff Prompt Rules

The prompt must:

- Start a discussion, not a command-only work order.
- Ask the receiving agent to do an extensive independent review before changing
  anything.
- Make clear that the receiving agent owns that review; the handoff only gives
  starting context and known constraints.
- Ask the agent to decide whether the task is a good idea, stale, already
  solved, over-scoped, or better handled differently.
- Assume the agent starts in the repo, a parent directory, a workspace directory,
  or a home directory and can find the repo itself.
- Avoid filesystem paths. No absolute paths, home-directory paths, checkout
  names, or repo-relative file paths unless the user explicitly requests them.
- Use portable anchors instead: repo owner/name, product/module names, issue/PR
  URLs, branch names, package/plugin names, public symbols, command names, config
  keys, exact error text, docs titles, and search terms.
- Include enough context for the receiving agent to get the right repo, boundary,
  and desired outcome.
- Include constraints, non-goals, validation expectations, and the desired
  output shape.
- Tell the receiving agent to re-check live repo/GitHub/CI state where relevant.
- Tell the receiving agent not to push, merge, close issues/PRs, label, or post
  public comments unless the handoff explicitly asks for it.

## Prompt Template

Use this shape by default:

```text
I want to discuss and possibly work on: <short task title>

Context:
- <portable repo/product context>
- <what triggered this task>
- <known current state, branch/issue/PR names or URLs if relevant>
- <important constraints and ownership boundaries>

Before doing any implementation:
- Find the right repository from the current directory, a parent directory, or the usual workspace.
- Read the local agent/repo instructions.
- Inspect the relevant code, docs, tests, recent commits, and linked issue/PR state.
- Decide whether this task is still real, whether the proposed direction is a good idea, and whether a smaller/better fix exists.
- Call out stale assumptions, hidden risks, and anything that should stop the work.

Task:
- <what to investigate or implement if the review supports it>
- <expected behavior or decision criteria>
- <non-goals>

Validation:
- <focused tests/checks/live proof expected>
- <what evidence should be included>
- <what is explicitly not required>

Output:
- Start with your review findings and recommendation.
- Then give the proposed plan or patch summary.
- If you edit code, keep changes scoped and report exact proof run.
- Do not push, merge, close issues/PRs, label, or post public comments unless explicitly told.
```

## Clipboard

On macOS:

```sh
pbcopy < /tmp/handoff-prompt.txt
```

Use a temp file or pipe. Avoid inline shell quoting for prompts containing
backticks, `$`, quotes, or user text.

If `pbcopy` is unavailable, use the obvious platform clipboard tool (`wl-copy`,
`xclip`, `clip.exe`) or print the prompt and say clipboard copy was unavailable.

## Quality Bar

- No invented facts. Mark reviewed facts as such only after checking them.
- No path leakage. Rewrite any accidental path as a symbol, module, command,
  issue/PR URL, or search term.
- Enough context for a fresh agent to orient; no giant brain dump.
- First real instruction to the receiving agent: review, discuss, assess.

## Step 2 of 2 · Sep 2 · Closing the remaining gaps

The first commit established the rule, but review found that the rule was not yet enforced everywhere.

**What changed since the last step:** The initial fix protected commit hooks and attach. The second step audited other operations that could write or realign checkpoint data.

Four gaps were found:

1. **Explain generation**

Read-only explain may discover a checkpoint from body text. But `--generate` saves a generated summary, so it must require a final trailer.

```text
Body mentions A
Final trailers contain B

Read explanation → may discover A
Generate summary → may write only to B
```

2. **Legacy migration**

Migration can change attribution state. It previously allowed a body occurrence to prove that an old session belonged to a checkpoint. That evidence was too weak for changing future attribution.

3. **Git trailer grammar**

This is not a real trailer:

```text
  Entire-Checkpoint: A
```

Leading whitespace makes it body or continuation text. However, indentation is valid after a real trailer:

```text
Notes: Long explanation
 continuation of the explanation
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

The parser therefore needed to distinguish a continuation from a new trailer.

4. **Commit comments**

Editor-created messages contain disposable comment lines:

```text
# Please enter the commit message...
```

But `#` can also be deliberate user content when supplied through `git commit -m` or `-F`.

That distinction matters here:

```text
Subject

Entire-Checkpoint: A
# actual user content
```

If Entire always deleted `# actual user content`, it would accidentally make `A` look like the final trailer block. The fix therefore considers both the Git-configured comment prefix and how the message was supplied.

The deeper lesson was:

> Defining a security boundary is insufficient; every operation that crosses it must use the correct parser and the correct preprocessing.

## Journey takeaways

- Discovery evidence and mutation authority require separate APIs.
- Valid syntax does not prove provenance, intent, or permission.
- A safety rule must be applied at the final write decision—not only in a shared parser.
- Preprocessing can silently change security meaning.
- Tests should exercise durable effects, such as which checkpoint was actually written, rather than only parser output.

Understanding check: why may ordinary `explain` use a body checkpoint while `explain --generate` may not?

content.text: and how do we know if it's a sqaush merge?
and how do we know if it's a sqaush merge?

We generally **cannot reliably know** that a commit is a squash merge.

A squash commit might look like:

```text
Combine login changes

First change
Entire-Checkpoint: AAA111

Second change
Entire-Checkpoint: BBB222
```

But a person could manually write exactly the same message:

```text
Combine login changes

First change
Entire-Checkpoint: AAA111

Second change
Entire-Checkpoint: BBB222
```

After the commit exists, those messages are identical. Git does not attach a trustworthy flag saying:

```text
This commit was created by a squash merge.
```

We could guess based on wording such as “Squashed commit,” but wording is customizable and easy to imitate. That would not be a safe rule.

So the solution deliberately avoids asking:

> “Is this a squash merge?”

Instead, it asks:

> “What is Entire about to do with the checkpoint ID?”

- If Entire is only searching history, checkpoint IDs anywhere in the message are accepted as **possible historical references**.
- If Entire is about to write or modify checkpoint data, only an ID in the final trailer section is accepted.

In short:

```text
We cannot reliably identify squash commits.

Therefore:

Body checkpoint → possible historical clue
Final trailer    → intended write target
```

This is also why checking whether the checkpoint exists is insufficient. A manually written message can name a real existing checkpoint just as easily as a genuine squash message can.

---
name: using-entire
user-invocable: true
disable-model-invocation: false
description: >
  Use for any codebase exploration or understanding task — reads historical
  intent from Entire checkpoints instead of guessing. Orchestrates other Entire
  skills to give the agent provenance-backed answers about code.
---

# Using Entire

Your default when exploring or understanding code should be: **read the
recorded intent, don't guess.**

Entire checkpoints capture the prompts, transcripts, and decisions behind every
agent-driven change. When you need to understand why code exists or how a module
evolved, look up the checkpoint history first. Only fall back to inference from
code structure when no history is available — and label that explicitly.

## When This Skill Activates

Use this skill whenever the task involves:

- Exploring or understanding an unfamiliar module or file
- Preparing to refactor, extend, or debug code you didn't write
- Answering "why is this like this?" or "what was the intent?"
- Doing pre-work research before making changes
- Any codebase exploration where historical context would help

Do **not** use this skill for simple, well-understood edits where you already
have full context (e.g. "add a comment to line 5").

## First Step: Check Repository Status

Before diving into specific lookups, check whether Entire is available and
the repository has checkpoint history:

```bash
entire status
```

This tells you whether Entire is enabled, which git hooks are installed, whether
the metadata branch is initialized, and any active sessions on the current
branch.

Also check whether the Entire Graph plugin is installed:

```bash
entire graph version
```

If it prints a version, the graph is available and **every code-locating step
in this skill must go through it** — never grep, find, or read whole files to
locate code when the graph can answer. The division of labor:

- **Structure** (where is X, what calls X, what breaks if X changes) → `entire graph`
- **Intent** (why is X like this, what was the developer thinking) → checkpoints

Graph command palette:

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --format agent --top-k 5 \
  --query "<task in one sentence>"                                            # locate
entire graph def <symbol>                                                     # one definition
entire graph neighbors --repo . --symbol X --relation CALLS --direction in --format agent  # callers
entire graph impact --repo . --symbol X --format text                         # blast radius
entire graph commit <ref>                                                     # entity-level change list
entire graph diff --base A --head B --json                                    # semantic changes between refs
```

One search, then act — answer from the search output when it already suffices,
and read only a focused line range around reported locations. Skip the graph
when the task already names one small exact file. The full measured doctrine
lives in the `lean-mode` skill.

Treat graph output as evidence, not an oracle: read focused source around the
reported `file:line` before relying on it. If `entire graph version` fails, the
plugin is absent — fall back to standard search tools without it.

## Scenario Routing

When this skill activates, determine which sub-skill best fits the user's need:

| Scenario | Typical user expressions | Delegate to |
|----------|------------------------|-------------|
| Locate or trace code structure | "where is X implemented" / "what calls X" / "what would changing X affect" / "find the code that does Y" | run `entire graph` directly (`search`, `def`, `neighbors`, `impact`) |
| Code block provenance | "why is this like this" / "wtf is going on" / "what happened at src/auth.ts:42" / "tell me why this changed" | `what-happened` |
| Find prior work | "has anyone done X before" / "search past work for rate limiting" / "find the previous implementation" | `search` |
| Recall a task playbook | "have we done this before" / "recall how we did X" / "how did we do this last time" | `recall` |
| Replay feature history | "replay <feature>" / "walk me through how X was built" / "show me the journey of Y" | `replay` |
| Teach a repo topic | "teach me <topic>" / "how does <topic> work in this repo" / "give me a lesson on X" | `entire-teach` |
| Understand original intent | "explain this function" / "explain parseConfig" / "what was the intent behind src/auth.ts" | `explain` |
| Generate a dispatch / summary | "summarize recent work" / "generate a dispatch" / "what was accomplished this week" | run `entire dispatch` directly |
| Code review with intent context | "review these changes" / "review this branch" / "audit before merging" | `entire-review` |
| Hand off to another agent | "hand off this session" / "continue in another agent" / "pick up the codex session" | `session-handoff` |
| Convert session to skill | "turn this into a skill" / "make a skill from this session" | `session-to-skill` |
| Link session to other repos | "link session to other repos" / "attach session to the foo repo" | `session-crosslink` |
| General exploration | "understand this module" / "explore how auth works" / "help me understand the codebase" | _(self — see below)_ |

If the scenario clearly maps to a sub-skill, delegate entirely to that skill's
workflow. Do not duplicate their steps here.

## General Exploration Flow

When no specific sub-skill fits — e.g. the user asks to "understand this
module" or "explore how auth works" — use this flow:

1. **Identify key files** in the target area with the graph when it is
   installed:

```bash
entire graph search --repo . --profile full --query "<the module or behavior to understand>"
```

Then map the neighborhood of the top hits (`neighbors` for callers,
`impact` for blast radius) instead of reading whole files. Without the graph
plugin, identify entry points, main types, and core functions manually.

2. **Check for checkpoint coverage** on each key file:

```bash
git log --format='%H %s' -5 -- <file>
```

Look for `Entire-Checkpoint:` trailers in the commit bodies:

```bash
git log --format='%H %b' -5 -- <file> | grep -B1 'Entire-Checkpoint:'
```

3. **Read intent for covered commits** — extract the checkpoint ID from the
   trailer, then use JSON output for non-interactive consumption:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --checkpoint <checkpoint-id> --json --no-pager
```

If you only have a commit hash (not a checkpoint ID), use:

```bash
entire checkpoint explain --commit <sha> --no-pager
```

4. **Synthesize**: combine the recorded intent (from checkpoints) with the
   current code structure to build a comprehensive understanding.

5. **Report** your findings, clearly distinguishing:
   - Facts backed by checkpoint transcripts (label as "recorded intent")
   - Observations inferred from code alone (label as "inferred from code")

## AI Agent Usage Notes

When running Entire commands from an agent subprocess:

- **Always pass `--json`** for commands that support it and might prompt
  interactively. `--json` implies non-interactive output.
- **Always pass `--no-pager`** to prevent pager activation in subprocess
  contexts.
- **Always specify `--checkpoint <id>` or `--commit <sha>`** for
  `entire checkpoint explain` — without a locator, the command falls back to an
  interactive picker.

## When No Checkpoints Exist

If the target code predates Entire or has no checkpoint coverage:

1. Say explicitly: "No Entire checkpoint history is available for this code."
2. Proceed with standard code understanding — still graph-first when the
   plugin is installed (`entire graph search` to locate, `neighbors`/`impact`
   to trace call sites), reading focused source around the results; check git
   log for history.
3. Label all explanations as "inferred from code — not backed by recorded
   intent."
4. If the user wants deeper history, suggest `search` with related keywords —
   there may be checkpoints on related work even if the specific file isn't
   directly covered.

## Transparency Principle

Always make it clear whether your answer comes from:

- **Checkpoint-backed history** — you read the actual session transcript and
  know the developer's stated intent
- **Code inference** — you analyzed the code structure and are reasoning about
  probable intent

Never present inferred intent as if it were recorded fact. The core value of
this workflow is that distinction.

## References

For a deeper understanding of Entire's capabilities beyond what the sub-skills
cover, consult these resources:

- **CLI help**: run `entire help` to see all available commands and flags
- **Documentation**: https://docs.entire.io/llms.txt — AI-friendly
  documentation index following the [llms.txt standard](https://llmstxt.org),
  designed to be consumed directly by LLMs and coding agents

content.text:
There are 12 changed files:

- 5 production files: trailer parsing, commit hooks, attach, explain, and migration.
- 7 test files proving those behaviors.

We’ll take them one at a time.

## File 1: `trailers.go`

[trailers.go](/Users/muskanpaliwal/Work/open-source/entire/cli/fix-checkpoint-trailer-block/cmd/entire/cli/trailers/trailers.go:106) is the central commit-message parser.

Previously, Entire effectively had one checkpoint parser:

```go
ParseCheckpoint(message)
```

It searched the entire message:

```text
Subject

Entire-Checkpoint: A

More body text
```

Result:

```text
Found A
```

That behavior is necessary for finding checkpoint history, but unsafe for choosing where to write data.

The file now provides two kinds of parser.

### Discovery parser

The existing functions remain:

```go
ParseCheckpoint(message)
ParseAllCheckpoints(message)
```

They search the whole message.

Use them when asking:

> “Which checkpoints are mentioned in this commit?”

This preserves squash-merge history.

### Mutation parser

Two new functions were added:

```go
ParseCheckpointFromFinalTrailerBlock(message)
ParseAllCheckpointsFromFinalTrailerBlock(message)
```

They inspect only the final metadata section.

Use them when asking:

> “Which checkpoint did this commit officially designate?”

For example:

```text
Subject

Entire-Checkpoint: A

More body text

Signed-off-by: Muskan <muskan@example.com>
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

The results are:

```text
Whole-message parser: A and B
Final-block parser:   B
```

So historical searching can find both, but a write operation may target only `B`.

### Trailer grammar was corrected

Indented text is not treated as a new trailer:

```text
  Entire-Checkpoint: A
```

But indentation is allowed as a continuation of a real trailer:

```text
Notes: This is a long note
 continued on another line
Entire-Checkpoint: B
```

The parser accepts the paragraph and finds only `B`.

`HasOPFApplied` was also moved onto the same strict final-block logic, so this body text no longer counts:

```text
  Entire-OPF-Applied: true
```

In simple terms, this file created the two rulebooks:

```text
Search rulebook → look everywhere
Write rulebook  → look only at official bottom metadata
```

Next file: `manual_commit_hooks.go`, where the commit lifecycle starts using the new write rulebook.
